# Partitions, QOS, and queue times

Where to send a job and how long you'll wait — the highest-leverage choices you make.

## Partitions and QOS on MedicineBow {#sec-partitions}

### Partition = which hardware

A partition is a named pool of nodes. Submit with `--partition=<name>` (the default is `mb`).

| Partition | Nodes | Cores/node | Mem/node | GPUs/node | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`mb`** *(default)* | 25 | 96 (EPYC 9454) | ~1023 GB | — | general CPU work |
| `mb-h100` | 6 | 96 | ~1281 GB | 8× **H100** | large model training, PINNs |
| `mb-l40s` | 4 | 96 | ~765 GB | 8× L40S¹ | inference, mid-size training |
| `mb-a30` | 8 | 96 | ~765 GB | 8× A30 | dev/GPU, smaller models |
| `mb-a6000` | 1 | 64 | ~1023 GB | 4× A6000 | GPU dev |
| `mb-r6000` | 3 | 72 | ~515 GB | 4× R6000 | GPU dev |
| `debug` | 4 | 28 | ~128 GB | — | quick tests (pair with `debug` QOS) |
| `teton` | ~250 | 32 | ~120 GB+ | — | large CPU throughput, arrays |
| `beartooth` | 9 | 56 | ~257 GB+ | — | CPU work |
| `wildiris` | 5 | 48 | ~507 GB+ | — | CPU work |
| `non-investor` | 110 | mixed | mixed | — | **CPU work you don't want preempted** |
| `non-investor-gpu` | 7 | mixed | mixed | mixed | **GPU work you don't want preempted** |
| `inv-*` | varies | varies | varies | varies | investor-owned; borrowable but **preemptible** |

<small>¹ One L40S node has 4 GPUs instead of 8. Numbers are the machine as observed in July 2026; verify current state with `showpartitions` and `sinfo`.</small>

The `inv-*` partitions are investor ("condo")
hardware: you can run on them when they're idle, but the owner can reclaim the node and
preempt your job (@sec-preemption).

::: {.callout-note}
## Avoiding preemption: use `non-investor`, not `--constraint`
`--constraint=non-investor` matches nothing on the current machine and does nothing. Use a
**partition** instead: `--partition=non-investor` (110 nodes) or
`--partition=non-investor-gpu` (7 GPU nodes; you must also request a GPU with `--gres=gpu:N`
there) stays on hardware that won't be reclaimed. This
is the right home for long, un-checkpointed runs.
:::

You can list several partitions and let Slurm use whichever frees up first;
`--partition=mb,teton,beartooth` is common for CPU throughput work.

### QOS = which service tier

A **Quality of Service** sets three things at once: your **maximum walltime**, your **CPU
footprint cap**, and your **priority**. Submit with `--qos=<name>` (the default is `normal`).

| QOS | Priority | Max walltime | CPU cap / account | Your project can use it? |
|---|---:|---|---:|:---:|
| `interactive` | 90 | 8 h | 4746 | ✅ |
| `fast` | 80 | 12 h | 4746 | ✅ |
| `normal` *(default)* | 70 | 3 d | 4746 | ✅ |
| `long` | 60 | 7 d | 2876 | ✅ |
| `debug` | 0 | 1 h | 7 cpu / 32 G / 2 nodes | ✅ |
| `extended` | 50 | 14 d | 2157 | ❌ (not granted) |
| `inv-*` (investor) | 110 | 14 d | varies | ❌ (owners only) |

Confirm your own list any time:

```bash
sacctmgr -n show assoc user=$USER format=qos
# <project>:  debug, fast, interactive, long, normal
sqos                         # full QOS table with limits
```

::: {.callout-important}
## The walltime trade-off
Longer requested walltime means lower priority and a smaller footprint cap. `fast` (12 h)
gives priority 80 and the full 4746-core cap; `long` (7 d) drops to priority 60 and a
~40%-smaller cap. This trade-off drives the recommendations in @sec-queue-times.
:::

### `DenyOnLimit`: rejected at submit

Every user-facing QOS is flagged **`DenyOnLimit`**. If you ask for more than a QOS allows — say a 5-day
run under `normal` (max 3 d), or more cores than the cap — Slurm rejects the job at submit
time with a clear error rather than queuing it indefinitely. Fix the request and resubmit.

### Putting both knobs in a script

```bash
#SBATCH --partition=mb          # hardware: general CPU nodes
#SBATCH --qos=fast              # tier: 12h max, high priority
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00         # within the fast 12h ceiling
```

For a GPU job:

```bash
#SBATCH --partition=mb-l40s
#SBATCH --qos=normal
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1            # ask for 1 GPU (see @sec-gpu)
#SBATCH --time=08:00:00
```

## Queue times: which partition for what {#sec-queue-times}

### What the queue looks like

At a representative midday moment on MedicineBow there were roughly **2,000 jobs running and
800 pending**. Almost every pending job's reason was `Priority` — the machine is busy and
you're in line, not that you asked for something impossible.

### Measured wait times (start minus eligible)

The table below is from **~1.7 million jobs over a recent 3-day window**, measured as the
time between a job becoming eligible and starting. Read it for order of magnitude, not as a
promise; your wait depends on how busy the machine is and how big your request is.

| Partition | Median wait | 90th percentile | Character |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `teton` | ~0 s | ~13 min | huge pool; throughput/array work starts fast |
| `mb` (default CPU) | <1 min | ~10 min | plentiful; short CPU jobs start quickly |
| `beartooth` | ~4 min | ~11 min | steady CPU capacity |
| `mb-a30` (GPU) | ~2 min | ~1.5 h | smaller GPUs, usually gettable |
| `mb-h100` (GPU) | seconds–hours | **~8–9 h** | **bimodal**: idle now, or a long wait |
| `mb-l40s` (GPU) | ~1 h | ~2–6 h | **consistently contended** |
| `beartooth-gpu` | ~1 h | ~7 h | contended |

By **QOS**, the CPU signal is even clearer:

| QOS | Median wait | 90th percentile |
|---|---:|---:|
| `interactive` | ~11 s | ~30 s |
| `fast` | ~0 s | ~13 min |
| `normal` | ~19 s | ~8 min |

::: {.callout-note}
## How to read these numbers
This window included a large `fast`-QOS job array on `teton`, which pulls the `teton`/`fast`
medians toward zero. The **`normal`-QOS row (tens of thousands of ordinary jobs: median
~19 s, 90th percentile ~8 min)** is the most representative figure for a normal CPU job. The
pattern holds either way: CPU work starts fast; GPU work, especially L40S/H100, is where you
wait. Measure the live picture before a big campaign — see the commands at the end of this
chapter.
:::

#### The longer view: wait times month by month

The tables above are a short snapshot. The figure below is the full history — every finished
job from June 2024 to July 2026, about **70 million** of them — as a box plot of wait time per
month, with the monthly job count underneath.

![Wait time (start − eligible) by month, June 2024 – July 2026. Boxes span the 25th–75th percentile with the median line; whiskers the 5th–95th. The lower panel is monthly job volume. Both axes that can be are log-scaled; 0-second waits sit at the 1-second floor.](img/wait-times-by-month.svg){#fig-monthly}

Two things stand out. Wait times **vary a lot month to month**: median waits range from about a
second in quiet, array-dominated months to tens of minutes when the machine is busy, and the
busiest months push the 90th percentile into hours. And the very low medians in the
high-volume recent months are the signature of large `fast`-QOS job arrays (@sec-arrays) that
start almost instantly — one well-behaved sweep can move the whole month's median. The planning
takeaway is unchanged: a normal CPU job usually starts within minutes, but *how busy the
machine is this month* matters, so check the live queue before a big campaign (end of chapter).

#### The same picture, split by partition

The heatmap below is those same 26 months broken out by partition — median wait on top,
90th percentile below. It's the visual form of the partition table: the CPU pools (`mb`,
`teton`, `beartooth`, `non-investor`) stay cool most months, while the GPU partitions —
especially `mb-l40s` and `mb-h100` — run hot, sometimes for months at a stretch.

![Wait time by month and partition: median (top) and 90th percentile (bottom). Warmer = longer wait; grey = fewer than 30 jobs that month. Log color scale.](img/wait-times-by-month-partition.svg){#fig-partition-heatmap}

(When you submit — hour of day or day of week — barely moves the needle by comparison: across
these 26 months the median wait is flat around a few seconds whenever you submit. Spend your
effort on the partition and QOS, not on timing.)

## Short proof-of-concept vs. long simulation

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-choose
%%| fig-cap: "Where to send a job. Short work wants a fast start (debug/interactive/fast); long work wants a big, non-preemptible pool (non-investor + long) and checkpointing."
flowchart TD
    Q{"What are you doing?"} --> T["Quick test: does it run?"]
    Q --> D["Interactive development"]
    Q --> N["Normal CPU job, under 3 days"]
    Q --> Lng["Long simulation, 3-7 days"]
    Q --> G["GPU work"]
    T --> Tp["partition debug + qos debug"]
    D --> Dp["partition mb + qos interactive"]
    N --> Np["partition mb or mb,teton + qos normal/fast"]
    Lng --> Lp["partition non-investor + qos long + checkpoint"]
    G --> Gq{"iterating or production?"}
    Gq -->|"dev"| Gd["partition mb-a30"]
    Gq -->|"production"| Gp["partition mb-h100 / mb-l40s"]
```

#### Short proof-of-concept / debugging / "does it even run?"

You want to start now, run briefly, and iterate. Priority and low wait matter; walltime and
footprint don't.

```bash
#SBATCH --partition=debug        # 4 dedicated test nodes, usually idle
#SBATCH --qos=debug              # 1 h max, but starts almost instantly
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=8G
```

- Use the **`debug` partition + `debug` QOS** for the fastest possible start on a tiny job
  (cap: 1 h, ≤2 nodes, ≤7 cores, ≤32 G).
- Need a bit more than debug allows but still want to start fast? Use **`fast` QOS on `mb`**
  (12 h ceiling, priority 80) — median start of seconds.
- Developing interactively? **`interactive` QOS** starts in ~10–30 s (@sec-interactive).
- For GPU proof-of-concept, develop on **`mb-a30`** (starts in minutes), *not* H100.

#### Long production simulation / big ensemble / final runs

You need days of walltime and want to avoid preemption, accepting a longer initial wait in
exchange for a long, stable run.

```bash
#SBATCH --partition=non-investor   # big pool that won't be reclaimed
#SBATCH --qos=long                 # up to 7 days
#SBATCH --time=5-00:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16
#SBATCH --mem=32G
```

- Use **`long` QOS** for multi-day runs (7 d ceiling). `normal` (3 d) is the default and
  fine for sub-3-day jobs.
- Submit to **`--partition=non-investor`** (CPU) or **`non-investor-gpu`** (GPU) so an
  investor can't reclaim your node mid-run. Or list several CPU partitions
  (`--partition=mb,teton,beartooth`) to start on whichever frees first — at the cost of
  possible preemption on `inv-*` hardware.
- **Checkpoint** (@sec-checkpointing) so a node failure, walltime overrun, or preemption
  doesn't cost you the whole run.
- Right-size first (@sec-resources): a leaner request under `long` starts sooner than a bloated one.

#### The quick decision table

| Your situation | Partition | QOS | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Does my script run at all?" | `debug` | `debug` | near-instant start, 1 h cap |
| Fast CPU test, up to 12 h | `mb` | `fast` | priority 80, full core cap, seconds to start |
| Interactive development | `mb` | `interactive` | ~10–30 s start, live shell |
| Normal CPU job, < 3 days | `mb` (or `mb,teton`) | `normal` | default; ~20 s median start |
| Long CPU simulation, 3–7 days | `non-investor` | `long` | big non-preemptible pool |
| GPU proof-of-concept | `mb-a30` | `normal` | GPUs you can usually get in minutes |
| GPU production / big training | `mb-h100` / `mb-l40s` | `normal`/`long` | most power; expect an hours-long wait |

### Check the live queue before you commit

Historical medians are a guide; the live machine is what matters. Before a big submission:

```bash
showpartitions               # idle vs busy nodes, per partition, right now
sinfo -p mb-h100 -o "%P %t %D"   # how many H100 nodes are idle this second?
gpuavail                     # ARCC helper: free GPUs by type
squeue -p mb-l40s            # how deep is the line for this partition?
showuserlimits               # what am I allowed to ask for?
```

If `showpartitions` shows idle H100 nodes, submit now. If the GPU partitions are full and the
line is long, either develop on `mb-a30` or submit and walk away.

Once a job is queued, `showjobreasons <jobid>` explains why it's still pending
(@sec-monitoring) — usually `Priority` (wait) or `Resources` (large request).

@sec-priority explains why QOS dominates your position in that line.

## How priority is computed {#sec-priority}

### The formula

Slurm computes a priority score for every pending job and runs the highest scores first
(subject to backfill, below). The score is a weighted sum; MedicineBow's weights are:

```text
PriorityWeightQOS       = 200     <- dominant
PriorityWeightFairShare = 100
PriorityWeightJobSize   = 100
PriorityWeightAge       = 10
PriorityWeightPartition = 0       (partition doesn't affect priority here)
```

Each factor is a number between 0 and 1, multiplied by its weight, and summed. The biggest
lever, by a wide margin, is **QOS**.

### What each factor means

**QOS (weight 200).** Higher-priority QOS means a better position. From @sec-partitions:
`interactive` (90) > `fast` (80) > `normal` (70) > `long` (60). Choosing `fast` over `long`
is worth more priority than any amount of waiting, which is why the short-vs-long decision in
@sec-queue-times matters.

**Fair-share (weight 100) — recent usage.** Slurm tracks how much your account has used
lately relative to its share. Heavy use this week lowers your fair-share factor, and thus your
priority, for a while; it recovers as usage decays (half-life ~7 days here). This mechanism
stops any one group from monopolizing the machine and rewards steady use over bursts.

**Job size (weight 100).** A factor based on the resources requested. With the
`SMALL_RELATIVE_TO_TIME` flag this cluster sets, it interacts with your time request — another
reason not to over-ask (@sec-resources).

**Age (weight 10) — time spent waiting.** A job gains priority the longer it sits, maxing out
after ~3 days. At weight 10, age is a tie-breaker, not a strategy; you won't age past someone
who chose a better QOS.

### Practical takeaway

::: {.callout-important}
## QOS dominates priority
Because QOS is weighted 2× fair-share and 20× age, the highest-leverage choice for start time
is the most appropriate high-priority QOS your job fits — the shortest walltime tier that
still lets it finish (@sec-queue-times). Waiting longer, resubmitting, or submitting at 3am
have little effect by comparison.
:::

### Backfill: why a small job can jump the line

Priority sets the order, but Slurm also **backfills**: if the top job is waiting for, say, 40
nodes to free up, Slurm slots a smaller, shorter job into the gap now, as long as that doesn't
delay the top job's reserved start time. This is why a 20-minute test can start immediately
even when the queue looks deep, and why short jobs start sooner than long ones. Requesting
less time and fewer resources makes your job backfill-eligible in more gaps — another payoff
for right-sizing.

### Seeing your own priority

```bash
sprio -j <jobid>            # the priority breakdown for a pending job
sprio -l                    # all pending jobs, with factor columns
showjobreasons <jobid>      # ARCC helper: plain-language "why am I waiting?"
```

If `sprio` shows a low QOS factor because you're on `long` but the job would finish in 10
hours, resubmitting under `fast` is the most effective change you can make.

Next: watching jobs run and diagnosing them when they don't (@sec-monitoring).
